summary: A 1976 discussion of the RCTE Telnet option, collected as a dialogue following the publication of RFC 718. It raises points on how the option is negotiated and on clearing input buffers.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a record of people emailing each other about how to make one Telnet feature work properly.

questions: how does rcte clear input buffer
subtitle: Notes on implementing the RCTE Telnet feature from RFC 718.

tldr.problem: RFC 718 introduced RCTE (Record Telnet Continuation Escape), but implementation teams found ambiguities in the negotiation protocol and needed a way to clear the input buffer during use.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC records a email discussion between implementers at BBN and SRI-ARC about the right way to negotiate RCTE mode and proposes using the synch-datamark sequence to clear input buffers and reset counters.
tldr.outcome: The discussion informed a revised RCTE specification. Key insights included requiring GO-AHEAD suppression, restoring ECHO state after RCTE, and clarifying RCTE interactions with other Telnet options.

today: RFC 719 is a historical record of implementation discussions that informed the development of the Telnet protocol. RCTE is now largely obsolete with modern terminal protocols, but the RFC preserves early implementation experience.

sections.title: RCTE Implementation Questions
sections.content: RFC 719 captures a dialogue among Telnet implementers following the publication of RFC 718, which defined the RCTE (Record Telnet Continuation Escape) option. The discussion focuses on two main issues: clarifying the negotiation sequence for enabling RCTE mode and solving the problem of clearing the input buffer when RCTE is active.
sections.plainLanguage: When teams tried to use the new Telnet feature, they ran into questions about how to turn it on and off properly.

sections.title: Mode Negotiation Protocol
sections.content: Implementers clarified that in normal RCTE negotiation, the server sends "WILL RCTE" and the user sends "DO RCTE". Nancy Mimno at BBN-NET noted that the reverse case (server sending "DO RCTE") requires explicit clarification that the user process must respond with "WILL" or "WON'T RCTE", and that this response serves as the synchronizing mark for the mode change.
sections.plainLanguage: The server and client need to agree before using the feature, and the agreement message marks the sync point.

sections.title: Clearing Input and Resetting State
sections.content: The group agreed that a "clear input and reset counters" function was necessary. The proposed solution uses the synch-datamark sequence, making this function a mandatory part of the RCTE option. Additionally, the Abort Output (AO) command should be interpreted as a request to send a synch-datamark when RCTE is active. The discussion also identified that RCTE interacts with other Telnet options: GO-AHEAD must be suppressed, ECHO mode must be restored after exiting RCTE, and BINARY mode is incompatible with RCTE.
sections.plainLanguage: They needed a way to clear out buffered keystrokes and reset counters, and figured out how to do it without breaking other Telnet features.

references.text: Postel, J., "RCTE - Remote Controlled Transmission Echo", RFC 718, July 1976.
